claim: Herd immunity arises during phage epidemics in structured Escherichia coli populations consisting of differing frequencies of susceptible and resistant cells harboring CRISPR immunity.
source: Here we experimentally demonstrate that herd immunity arises during phage epidemics in structured and unstructured Escherichia coli populations consisting of differing frequencies of susceptible and resistant cells harboring CRISPR immunity.
evidence: The abstract states this as a main finding of the experimental work, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Herd immunity arises during phage epidemics in unstructured Escherichia coli populations consisting of differing frequencies of susceptible and resistant cells harboring CRISPR immunity.
source: Here we experimentally demonstrate that herd immunity arises during phage epidemics in structured and unstructured Escherichia coli populations consisting of differing frequencies of susceptible and resistant cells harboring CRISPR immunity.
evidence: The abstract states this as a main finding of the experimental work, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Herd immunity in bacterial populations is affected by spatial population structure.
source: In addition, we develop a mathematical model that quantifies how herd immunity is affected by spatial population structure, bacterial growth rate, and phage replication rate.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the mathematical model, which is supported by both experimental data and theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Herd immunity in bacterial populations is affected by bacterial growth rate.
source: In addition, we develop a mathematical model that quantifies how herd immunity is affected by spatial population structure, bacterial growth rate, and phage replication rate.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the mathematical model, which is supported by both experimental data and theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Herd immunity in bacterial populations is affected by phage replication rate.
source: In addition, we develop a mathematical model that quantifies how herd immunity is affected by spatial population structure, bacterial growth rate, and phage replication rate.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the mathematical model, which is supported by both experimental data and theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Herd immunity may be important in bacterial communities, allowing for stable coexistence of bacteria and their phages.
source: Our experimental and theoretical findings indicate that herd immunity may be important in bacterial communities, allowing for stable coexistence of bacteria and their phages and the maintenance of polymorphism in bacterial immunity.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the findings in the abstract, based on inference from the experimental and theoretical results.

claim: Herd immunity may be important in bacterial communities, allowing for the maintenance of polymorphism in bacterial immunity.
source: Our experimental and theoretical findings indicate that herd immunity may be important in bacterial communities, allowing for stable coexistence of bacteria and their phages and the maintenance of polymorphism in bacterial immunity.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the findings in the abstract, based on inference from the experimental and theoretical results.

claim: Experimental research into herd immunity has focused mostly on mammals.
source: Experimental research into the phenomenon has focused mostly on mammals (Jeltsch et al., 1997; Mariner et al., 2012), birds (van Boven et al., 2008; Meister et al., 2008), and invertebrates (Konrad et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on mammals.

claim: Experimental research into herd immunity has focused mostly on birds.
source: Experimental research into the phenomenon has focused mostly on mammals (Jeltsch et al., 1997; Mariner et al., 2012), birds (van Boven et al., 2008; Meister et al., 2008), and invertebrates (Konrad et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on birds.

claim: Experimental research into herd immunity has focused mostly on invertebrates.
source: Experimental research into the phenomenon has focused mostly on mammals (Jeltsch et al., 1997; Mariner et al., 2012), birds (van Boven et al., 2008; Meister et al., 2008), and invertebrates (Konrad et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on invertebrates.

claim: The principles of herd immunity were employed to limit epidemics of pathogens through vaccination programs in human populations.
source: In human populations the principles of herd immunity were employed to limit epidemics of pathogens through vaccination programs (Fine et al., 2011), which in the case of smallpox lead to its eradication between 1959 and 1977 (Fenner, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fine et al., 2011.

claim: Vaccination programs employing herd immunity principles led to the eradication of smallpox between 1959 and 1977.
source: In human populations the principles of herd immunity were employed to limit epidemics of pathogens through vaccination programs (Fine et al., 2011), which in the case of smallpox lead to its eradication between 1959 and 1977 (Fenner, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fenner, 1993.

claim: Little work has focused on the potential role of herd immunity in microbial systems.
source: Interestingly, little work has focused on the potential role of herd immunity in microbial systems which contain a number of immune defense systems and have an abundance of phage pathogens.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the state of the field, implicitly supported by the lack of citations to such work.

claim: Bacteria have evolved multiple immune defense systems against phage pathogens.
source: Interestingly, little work has focused on the potential role of herd immunity in microbial systems which contain a number of immune defense systems and have an abundance of phage pathogens.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about bacterial immune systems.

claim: Bacteria have evolved early defense mechanisms that include the prevention of phage adsorption by blocking of phage receptors.
source: Early defense mechanisms include the prevention of phage adsorption by blocking of phage receptors (Nordström and Forsgren, 1974), production of an extracellular matrix (Hammad, 1998; Sutherland et al., 2004), or the excretion of competitive inhibitors (Destoumieux-Garzón et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nordström and Forsgren, 1974.

claim: Bacteria have evolved early defense mechanisms that include production of an extracellular matrix.
source: Early defense mechanisms include the prevention of phage adsorption by blocking of phage receptors (Nordström and Forsgren, 1974), production of an extracellular matrix (Hammad, 1998; Sutherland et al., 2004), or the excretion of competitive inhibitors (Destoumieux-Garzón et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hammad, 1998 and Sutherland et al., 2004.

claim: Bacteria have evolved early defense mechanisms that include the excretion of competitive inhibitors.
source: Early defense mechanisms include the prevention of phage adsorption by blocking of phage receptors (Nordström and Forsgren, 1974), production of an extracellular matrix (Hammad, 1998; Sutherland et al., 2004), or the excretion of competitive inhibitors (Destoumieux-Garzón et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Destoumieux-Garzón et al., 2005.

claim: Bacteria have evolved innate immune systems that include host restriction-modification systems (RMS).
source: Alongside these bacteria have evolved innate immune systems that target phage genomes for destruction. These include host restriction-modification systems (RMS) (Blumenthal and Cheng, 2002), argonaute-based RNAi-like systems (Swarts et al., 2014), and bacteriophage-exclusion (BREX) systems (Goldfarb et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Blumenthal and Cheng, 2002.

claim: Bacteria have evolved innate immune systems that include argonaute-based RNAi-like systems.
source: Alongside these bacteria have evolved innate immune systems that target phage genomes for destruction. These include host restriction-modification systems (RMS) (Blumenthal and Cheng, 2002), argonaute-based RNAi-like systems (Swarts et al., 2014), and bacteriophage-exclusion (BREX) systems (Goldfarb et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Swarts et al., 2014.

claim: Bacteria have evolved innate immune systems that include bacteriophage-exclusion (BREX) systems.
source: Alongside these bacteria have evolved innate immune systems that target phage genomes for destruction. These include host restriction-modification systems (RMS) (Blumenthal and Cheng, 2002), argonaute-based RNAi-like systems (Swarts et al., 2014), and bacteriophage-exclusion (BREX) systems (Goldfarb et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Goldfarb et al., 2015.

claim: Bacteria have evolved an adaptive immune system called CRISPR-Cas.
source: In addition to innate systems, bacteria have evolved an adaptive immune system called CRISPR-Cas (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat) (Sorek et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sorek et al., 2013.

claim: For immune systems to provide herd immunity, they must prevent further spread of the pathogen.
source: In order for any of these immune systems to provide herd immunity, they must prevent further spread of the pathogen.
evidence: This is stated as a logical requirement for herd immunity.

claim: The RMS, BREX, argonaute-based RNAi-like, and CRISPR-Cas systems degrade foreign phage DNA after it is injected into the cell.
source: Unlike the early defense mechanisms that may simply prevent an infection but not the further reproduction of infectious particles, the RMS, BREX, argonaute-based RNAi-like, and the CRISPR-Cas systems degrade foreign phage DNA after it is injected into the cell, and thus continue to remove phage particles from the environment, which increases their potential to provide herd immunity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these immune systems.

claim: The RMS, BREX, argonaute-based RNAi-like, and CRISPR-Cas systems continue to remove phage particles from the environment, which increases their potential to provide herd immunity.
source: Unlike the early defense mechanisms that may simply prevent an infection but not the further reproduction of infectious particles, the RMS, BREX, argonaute-based RNAi-like, and the CRISPR-Cas systems degrade foreign phage DNA after it is injected into the cell, and thus continue to remove phage particles from the environment, which increases their potential to provide herd immunity.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the mechanism of action of these immune systems.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas system is adaptive allowing cells to acquire immunity upon infection.
source: In addition to this, the CRISPR-Cas system is unique in that it is adaptive allowing cells to acquire immunity upon infection (see Figure 1A,B and C), which can lead to polymorphism in immunity even if the system is chromosomal.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CRISPR-Cas and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas system can lead to polymorphism in immunity even if the system is chromosomal.
source: In addition to this, the CRISPR-Cas system is unique in that it is adaptive allowing cells to acquire immunity upon infection (see Figure 1A,B and C), which can lead to polymorphism in immunity even if the system is chromosomal.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the adaptive nature of CRISPR-Cas.

claim: The reproductive rate of phage depends strongly on the physiology of the host bacterium.
source: In addition to immune system-specific factors, the reproductive rate of phage depends strongly on the physiology of the host bacterium (Hadas et al., 1997), and the underlying effective contact network which may vary greatly in bacterial populations depending on the details of their habitat.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hadas et al., 1997.

claim: The reproductive rate of phage depends on the underlying effective contact network which may vary greatly in bacterial populations depending on the details of their habitat.
source: In addition to immune system-specific factors, the reproductive rate of phage depends strongly on the physiology of the host bacterium (Hadas et al., 1997), and the underlying effective contact network which may vary greatly in bacterial populations depending on the details of their habitat.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about factors affecting phage reproduction.

claim: A resistant E. coli strain was engineered by introducing the CRISPR-Cas Type II system from Streptococcus pyogenes with a spacer targeting the T7 phage genome.
source: We engineered a resistant E. coli strain by introducing the CRISPR-Cas Type II system from Streptococcus pyogenes with a spacer targeting the T7 phage genome (see Material and Methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental construction of the resistant strain.

claim: The engineered CRISPR-Cas system confers a significant level of resistance to T7 phage as measured by the probability of cell burst when exposed to T7.
source: We find a significant level of resistance as measured by the probability of cell burst when exposed to T7 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding and is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Resistance conferred by the engineered CRISPR-Cas system is not fully penetrant as approximately 1 in 1000 resistant cells succumb to infection.
source: However, resistance is not fully penetrant as approximately 1 in 1000 resistant cells succumb to infection.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: As phage load increases (multiplicity of infection, MOI) the probability that a resistant cell bursts increases.
source: In addition, we observe that as phage load increases (multiplicity of infection, MOI) the probability that a cell bursts increases (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation and is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Upon infection, the resistant strain's cell growth is halted, yet the cell still adsorbs and degrades phages.
source: In order to determine the herd immunity threshold in our experimental system, we constructed the resistant strain such that upon infection the cell growth is halted, yet the cell still adsorbs and degrades phages (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is stated as a property of the engineered resistant strain and is shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: When the percentage of resistant individuals is in excess of 99.6% all 16 replicate populations survive a phage epidemic.
source: When the percentage of resistant individuals is in excess of 99.6% all 16 replicate populations survive a phage epidemic (i.e., show no detectable difference in growth profiles to the phage free controls; Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result and is shown in Figure 3.

claim: Populations with 99.2% resistant individuals show intermediate probabilities of survival with 10 out of 16 replicate populations surviving.
source: Populations with 99.2% and 98.4% resistant individuals show intermediate probabilities of survival – 10 out of 16 replicate populations and 4 out of 16 replicate populations survive, respectively (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result and is shown in Figure 3.

claim: Populations with 98.4% resistant individuals show intermediate probabilities of survival with 4 out of 16 replicate populations surviving.
source: Populations with 99.2% and 98.4% resistant individuals show intermediate probabilities of survival – 10 out of 16 replicate populations and 4 out of 16 replicate populations survive, respectively (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result and is shown in Figure 3.

claim: When populations have fewer than 96.9% resistant individuals all 16 replicate populations fail to survive and collapse under the epidemic.
source: However, when populations have fewer than 96.9% resistant individuals all 16 replicate populations fail to survive and collapse under the epidemic (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result and is shown in Figure 3.

claim: Bacterial growth was altered by reducing the concentration of nutrients in the medium by mixing LB broth with 1X M9 salts in different ratios.
source: To test this we altered bacterial growth by reducing the concentration of nutrients in the medium by mixing LB broth with 1X M9 salts in different ratios (Figure 4), which concurrently alters the T7 phage's latent period and burst size (Figure 5A,B and Table 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation and is shown in Figure 4.

claim: Reducing the concentration of nutrients in the medium concurrently alters the T7 phage's latent period and burst size.
source: To test this we altered bacterial growth by reducing the concentration of nutrients in the medium by mixing LB broth with 1X M9 salts in different ratios (Figure 4), which concurrently alters the T7 phage's latent period and burst size (Figure 5A,B and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation and is shown in Figures 5A, 5B and Table 1.

claim: As bacterial growth rates decline the fraction of resistant individuals necessary for population survival decreases.
source: Indeed, we observe as bacterial growth rates decline the fraction of resistant individuals necessary for population survival decreases (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation and is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When populations are grown in a 50% diluted growth medium, the fraction of resistant individuals required for a 100% probability of survival is 99.2%.
source: When the populations are grown in a 50% diluted growth medium, the fraction of resistant individuals required for a 100% probability of survival is 99.2%; when the fraction of resistant individuals is 75% or less populations go extinct.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: When populations are grown in a 50% diluted growth medium and the fraction of resistant individuals is 75% or less, populations go extinct.
source: When the populations are grown in a 50% diluted growth medium, the fraction of resistant individuals required for a 100% probability of survival is 99.2%; when the fraction of resistant individuals is 75% or less populations go extinct.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: In a 20% growth medium the fraction of resistant individuals required for survival decreases to 96.9%.
source: In a 20% growth medium the fraction of resistant individuals required for survival decreases to 96.9%, while the fraction when all replicates collapse to 50%.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: In a 20% growth medium the fraction of resistant individuals when all replicates collapse is 50%.
source: In a 20% growth medium the fraction of resistant individuals required for survival decreases to 96.9%, while the fraction when all replicates collapse to 50%.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: A decline in the number of plaque forming units is observed as the proportion of resistant individuals in the populations increases.
source: We observe a decline in the number of plaque forming units (see Appendix 2—figure 1) and a significant decrease in final plaque sizes as the proportion of resistant individuals in the populations increases (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation and is shown in Appendix 2—figure 1.

claim: A significant decrease in final plaque sizes is observed as the proportion of resistant individuals in the populations increases.
source: We observe a decline in the number of plaque forming units (see Appendix 2—figure 1) and a significant decrease in final plaque sizes as the proportion of resistant individuals in the populations increases (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation and is shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: When the fraction of resistant individuals exceeds 40%, the reduction in the speed of the spread is statistically significant immediately after the plaques are visually detectable.
source: In fact, when the fraction of resistant individuals exceeds 40%, the reduction in the speed of the spread is statistically significant immediately after the plaques are visually detectable (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation and is shown in Figure 7.

claim: All populations with low percentages of resistant individuals (below 40%) in liquid environment collapsed, indicating that spatial structure plays a role in herd immunity.
source: It should be noted that all populations with such low percentages of resistant individuals in liquid environment collapsed, indicating that spatial structure plays a role in herd immunity.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from comparing the liquid and plate experiments.

claim: Herd immunity is strongly influenced by spatial organization of the population.
source: We also observe that herd immunity is strongly influenced by spatial organization of the population, Figure 6.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Herd immunity can occur in phage-bacterial communities.
source: We show that herd immunity can occur in phage-bacterial communities and that it strongly depends on bacterial growth rates and spatial population structure.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion from the experimental and theoretical work.

claim: Herd immunity in phage-bacterial communities strongly depends on bacterial growth rates.
source: We show that herd immunity can occur in phage-bacterial communities and that it strongly depends on bacterial growth rates and spatial population structure.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion from the experimental and theoretical work.

claim: Herd immunity in phage-bacterial communities strongly depends on spatial population structure.
source: We show that herd immunity can occur in phage-bacterial communities and that it strongly depends on bacterial growth rates and spatial population structure.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion from the experimental and theoretical work.

claim: Bacterial populations in the wild are highly structured, as bacteria readily form micro-colonies or biofilms.
source: Furthermore, bacterial populations in the wild are also highly structured, as bacteria readily form micro-colonies or biofilms (Hall-Stoodley et al., 2004) and grow in spatially heterogeneous environments such as soil or the vertebrate gut (Fierer and Jackson, 2006), a second condition we have shown to facilitate herd immunity.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hall-Stoodley et al., 2004.

claim: Bacteria grow in spatially heterogeneous environments such as soil or the vertebrate gut.
source: Furthermore, bacterial populations in the wild are also highly structured, as bacteria readily form micro-colonies or biofilms (Hall-Stoodley et al., 2004) and grow in spatially heterogeneous environments such as soil or the vertebrate gut (Fierer and Jackson, 2006), a second condition we have shown to facilitate herd immunity.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fierer and Jackson, 2006.

claim: Spatial structure in bacterial populations facilitates herd immunity.
source: Furthermore, bacterial populations in the wild are also highly structured, as bacteria readily form micro-colonies or biofilms (Hall-Stoodley et al., 2004) and grow in spatially heterogeneous environments such as soil or the vertebrate gut (Fierer and Jackson, 2006), a second condition we have shown to facilitate herd immunity.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Herd immunity may be fairly prevalent in low nutrient communities such as soil and oligotrophic marine environments.
source: These suggest that herd immunity may be fairly prevalent in low nutrient communities such as soil and oligotrophic marine environments.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: While complete selective sweeps result in the reduction of genetic diversity at linked loci, herd immunity may lead to only partial selective sweeps in which some diversity is maintained.
source: First, while complete selective sweeps result in the reduction of genetic diversity at linked loci, herd immunity may lead to only partial selective sweeps in which some diversity is maintained.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about the evolutionary implications of herd immunity.

claim: Herd immunity has a potential to generate and maintain polymorphism at immunity loci, as has been shown for genes coding for the major histocompatibility complex (MHC).
source: Second, herd immunity has a potential to generate and maintain polymorphism at immunity loci, as has been shown for genes coding for the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) (Wills and Green, 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wills and Green, 1995.

claim: Polymorphism in CRISPR spacer contents have been demonstrated in various bacterial populations and communities.
source: Polymorphism in CRISPR spacer contents have been demonstrated in various bacterial (Tyson and Banfield, 2008; Sun et al., 2016; Kuno et al., 2014) and Archaeal (Held et al., 2010) populations and communities (Pride et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2013; Andersson and Banfield, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Polymorphism in CRISPR spacer contents have been demonstrated in various Archaeal populations.
source: Polymorphism in CRISPR spacer contents have been demonstrated in various bacterial (Tyson and Banfield, 2008; Sun et al., 2016; Kuno et al., 2014) and Archaeal (Held et al., 2010) populations and communities (Pride et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2013; Andersson and Banfield, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Held et al., 2010.

claim: Observed polymorphisms in CRISPR spacer content may result from frequency-dependent selection on resistance loci arising from herd immunity.
source: While these studies primarily explain polymorphisms in CRISPR spacer content as a result of rapid simultaneous independent acquisition of new spacers, we suggest that observed polymorphisms may result from frequency-dependent selection on resistance loci arising from herd immunity.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about an alternative explanation for observed polymorphisms.

claim: Considering the large population sizes of bacteria, drift is unlikely to have a strong effect, allowing herd immunity to maintain a large fraction of immunity polymorphism.
source: However, considering the large population sizes of bacteria, drift is unlikely to have a strong effect, allowing herd immunity to maintain a large fraction of immunity polymorphism.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on population genetics principles.

claim: Herd immunity might favor coexistence between hosts and their pathogens.
source: It has also been suggested that herd immunity might favor coexistence between hosts and their pathogens (Hamer, 1906), which can lead to cycling in pathogen incidence and proportions of resistant and susceptible individuals over time, e.g., in measles before the era of vaccination (Fine, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hamer, 1906 and Fine, 1993.

claim: Herd immunity can lead to cycling in pathogen incidence and proportions of resistant and susceptible individuals over time, e.g., in measles before the era of vaccination.
source: It has also been suggested that herd immunity might favor coexistence between hosts and their pathogens (Hamer, 1906), which can lead to cycling in pathogen incidence and proportions of resistant and susceptible individuals over time, e.g., in measles before the era of vaccination (Fine, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fine, 1993.

claim: A computer simulation study of coevolution of Streptococcus thermophilus and its phage found both cycling and stable coexistence of different CRISPR spacer mutants and phage strains.
source: In turn, a computer simulation study of coevolution of Streptococcus thermophilus and its phage found both cycling and stable coexistence of different CRISPR spacer mutants and phage strains (Childs et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Childs et al., 2014.

claim: When the MOI is large even resistant cells become susceptible to lysis resulting in the release of phage progeny.
source: However, when the MOI is large even resistant cells become susceptible to lysis resulting in the release of phage progeny (see Figure 2) (Westra et al., 2015; Chabas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 2 and citations to Westra et al., 2015 and Chabas et al., 2016.

claim: The two state model (constant growth rate while nutrients are present and no growth after depletion) describes the observed population trajectories in experiments sufficiently well.
source: Such a two state model – constant growth rate while nutrients are present and no growth after depletion – describes the observed population trajectories in experiments sufficiently well (see Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing model predictions to experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The model correctly captures the dependence of the herd immunity threshold on bacterial and phage growth parameters.
source: This verification of our model shows that it correctly captures the dependence of the herd immunity threshold on bacterial and phage growth parameters.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing model predictions to experimental observations.

claim: The inherent stochasticity of the adsorption process provides additional uncertainty not captured by the depicted error bars.
source: The inherent stochasticity of the adsorption process thus provides additional uncertainty, which is not captured by the depicted error bars.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about sources of uncertainty in the experiments.

claim: The fate of the population is more prone to stochastic effects as the phage replication rate is slower than in a fast growing population.
source: This additional stochasticity can explain wider transition zone in experiments with slower growing populations (dilution 0.5 and 0.2), because the fate of the population is more prone to stochastic effects as the phage replication rate is slower than in a fast growing population.
evidence: This is stated as an inference to explain experimental observations.

claim: At large MOIs the CRISPR-Cas system fails to provide effective immunity.
source: The density of phages behind the expanding front is large and as previously noted at large MOIs the CRISPR-Cas system fails to provide effective immunity (see section Materials and methods and appendix Infection load and efficiency of the CRISPR/Cas system).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: The structured environment effectively limits transit of phage from within a plaque to the expanding front.
source: However, in comparison to an un-structured environment (e.g., liquid) the structured environment effectively limits transit of phage from within a plaque to the expanding front: The combined effect of growth and diffusion usually generates a much faster expansion of phages during plaque formation, than diffusion alone.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about the effect of spatial structure.

claim: When nutrients are depleted, pure diffusion processes can explain the slow decrease in speed observed in experiments.
source: Only when nutrients are depleted, can pure diffusion processes explain the slow decrease in speed observed in experiments (see Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of experimental observations shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Predictions of the model show a discrepancy from experimental results on plates after depletion.
source: Predictions of our model show a discrepancy from experimental results on plates after depletion.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the model's limitations.
